text: By default, every Python object stores its attributes in a hidden dictionary, which is flexible but costly.
Defining dunder-slots tells Python the exact, fixed set of attributes this class will ever have.
Here Point promises only x and y, nothing more.
[chuckle] The object still works normally — you set and read x and y just like any class.
[sniff] But now try to add a new attribute z, and Python blocks it with an AttributeError.
That actually catches a common bug — a typo'd attribute name that would otherwise silently create garbage.
[sigh] The real win is memory — slotted objects skip the per-instance dictionary entirely.
When you're creating millions of small objects, that saving becomes dramatic, and access is faster too.
[groan] Use slots for tiny, numerous, fixed-shape objects — you trade a little flexibility for big efficiency gains.
